idiom_name: discriminated union on a literal tag + never-based exhaustiveness check
implementation_notes: TypeScript's realization is the discriminated union: a union of object types that all share one literal tag property (kind/status/type), so checking the tag narrows the value to exactly one member and the other members' fields are inaccessible. Exhaustiveness is expressed by letting the remaining value narrow to never - a default branch calling an assertNever(value: never) helper, or const check: never = value - so adding a variant breaks every switch that does not handle it. Keep the tag a literal type (never string), declare the union once and export it, and validate untrusted input at the boundary because the types are erased at run time and JSON.parse returns any.
pitfalls: A discriminant typed as string (or an enum widened to it) does not narrow: every variant must use a literal type, and interfaces used as union members can be reopened by declaration merging, silently adding fields.

Structural typing accepts a look-alike object that was never built as a variant (extra properties pass when the value is not a fresh literal), so values arriving from JSON or any must still be validated by a schema at the boundary.
Types are erased: nothing checks at run time, and a non-exhaustive switch without the never check compiles and returns undefined for the unhandled variant.
